chunks: And indeed, we were with the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family),

we would kill our fathers, sons, brothers, and uncles; this did not increase us except in faith and submission, and perseverance on the path, and patience over the pangs of pain, and zeal in fighting the enemy,
and indeed, a man from us and another from our enemy would pounce upon each other like two strong bulls, exchanging blows with each other, seeing which one would give his companion the cup of death,
so sometimes our man prevailed over the enemy, and sometimes the enemy's man prevailed over ours.

key_terms.تَصَاوُلَ: mutual pouncing or striking, like bulls
key_terms.مَضَضِ الْأَلَمِ: the pangs or bitterness of pain

ai.seo_question: How did fighting relatives affect the faith of the early Muslims according to Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: This narration from Nahj al-Balagha, delivered by Imam Ali (AS), contextualizes the early Muslim experience of *Qatl al-Aqarib* (killing close relatives) not as a tragedy but as a catalyst for deepening *Iman* and *Taslim* (submission). It vividly illustrates the brutal nature of single combat (*tasaful*), where warriors sought to kill each other, demonstrating the fluctuating fortunes of battle and the resilience required in the path of jihad.
